lesson.title: Breaking the Rule of Eight: Expanded Octets
lesson.summary: Some atoms, especially those from period 3 and beyond, can be surrounded by more than eight electrons in a stable Lewis structure, a pattern called an expanded octet.
lesson.body:
The octet rule, that atoms are most stable with 8 electrons around them, is really a guideline built on the behavior of second row elements like carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine, whose valence electrons live only in the 2s and 2p subshells, which together hold a maximum of 8 electrons. Elements in period 3 and beyond have an additional subshell available in their valence shell, the 3d subshell, alongside 3s and 3p. That extra room is why some period 3 and higher atoms can comfortably sit at the center of a structure with 10, 12, or even more electrons around them, a pattern called an expanded octet.

Sulfur hexafluoride, SF6, is a clean example. Total valence electrons: sulfur contributes 6, and six fluorines contribute 7 each, 42, for 6 plus 42 equals 48. Sulfur forms six S-F single bonds, using 12 electrons, which leaves 48 minus 12 equals 36 electrons for lone pairs, exactly 3 lone pairs, 6 electrons, on each of the six fluorines. Sulfur itself ends up with 6 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, meaning 12 electrons surround it, well beyond the usual 8.

Phosphorus pentachloride, PCl5, works the same way. Phosphorus contributes 5 valence electrons and five chlorines contribute 7 each, 35, for 40 total. Five P-Cl single bonds use 10 electrons, leaving 30 electrons for lone pairs, 3 lone pairs, 6 electrons, on each chlorine. Phosphorus ends up surrounded by 10 electrons from its 5 bonding pairs, another clear expanded octet. Chemists often describe this expanded bonding using hybridization labels such as sp3d for a 5 bonding pair center like phosphorus in PCl5, or sp3d2 for a 6 bonding pair center like sulfur in SF6, language you will see again when you study molecular geometry and hybridization in more depth. Xenon, a noble gas, forms expanded octet compounds too, such as XeF4, where four bonding pairs and two lone pairs surround the central xenon for a total of 12 electrons, a striking example from an element once assumed to be entirely unreactive.

Only atoms with an accessible valence d subshell can do this, which is why expanded octets show up for elements like sulfur, phosphorus, chlorine, and xenon, but never for second row elements like carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen, no matter how many atoms seem to be trying to bond to them. It is worth knowing that the exact mechanism behind expanded octets is more nuanced than electrons simply moving into d orbitals: modern bonding models suggest the larger atomic size and increased polarizability of period 3 and higher atoms play a significant role too. For everyday Lewis structure work, though, the practical rule holds: check an atom's period before assuming it must stop at 8 electrons.

Expanded octets connect directly back to the octet rule you already know and to subshell structure: you are simply recognizing that the rule of eight was never a law of physics, just a consequence of which subshells are available to hold electrons. Once a 3d subshell or higher is available in principle, an atom's true capacity depends on its size and how many other atoms can physically fit around it, which is why SF6 exists but a hypothetical, unrealistically crowded, six fluorine compound of oxygen does not.
